title: Request Priority & Hinting Protocol Playbook
author: Aisha Martinez
body:
Overview

This playbook defines a lightweight, backwards-compatible Request Priority & Hinting Protocol (RPHP) for Redwood internal services and external API-facing endpoints. The goal is to give clients safe, machine-readable signals to help the system make scheduling, queuing, and graceful-degradation decisions while preserving observable billing and correctness guarantees.

Motivation

- Services often need to make tradeoffs between latency and cost when capacity is constrained.
- Explicit priority signals from callers improve fairness and reduce tail-latency by letting the runtime schedule work more efficiently.
- Hints reduce inefficient client-side retries and tight coupling between client logic and server-side load-shedding policies.

Goals

1. Minimal impact on existing request schemas (single optional header + optional JSON envelope).
2. Deterministic server behavior based on hint values.
3. Measurable effects (metrics) to evaluate feature adoption and performance impact.
4. Granular client guidance for request composition and retry/backoff.

Protocol summary

- Transport: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, gRPC (metadata headers).
- Client hint: X-Redwood-Priority (string) — recommended values: realtime, interactive, standard, bulk, background.
- Optional JSON envelope in request body: "priority_hint" and "max_latency_ms" — used when header-level expressivity is insufficient (e.g., multi-task batch requests).
- Server response headers: X-Redwood-Accepted-Priority, X-Redwood-Queue-Estimate-ms, X-Redwood-Fallback-Policy.

Priority semantics

- realtime: Strict latency SLOs, small token budgets, no batching unless pre-warmed. Use only for single-turn transactional requests.
- interactive: Low latency but tolerant to minor batching (e.g., 10–50ms). Suitable for UI-driven flows and chat messages.
- standard: Default path for most API calls. Balanced latency/cost.
- bulk: High throughput, tolerant to batching and higher latency. Prefer async job endpoints.
- background: Lowest priority; may be queued or deferred indefinitely. Good for maintenance, garbage, or telemetry upload.

Request field table (recommended canonical fields)

| Field | Location | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| X-Redwood-Priority | HTTP header / gRPC metadata | string | One of the recommended values. Fall back to "standard" if absent. |
| priority_hint | JSON body (optional) | string | Same semantics as header when header cannot be set. |
| max_latency_ms | JSON body (optional) | integer | Client-specified upper bound on acceptable latency in ms. Server converts to SLO class for scheduling. |
| preserve_order | JSON body (optional) | boolean | For batch requests; when true, server avoids reordering across items in the same batch. |

Server behavior (must)

1. Defaulting: If no priority provided, treat as "standard".
2. Admission control: When under load, services should consult a priority-aware admission controller that consults current utilization, queue depth, and configured SLO curves.
3. Queueing & scheduling: Maintain separate internal queues per priority class. Implement elastic windowing to avoid starvation: background/bulk drains at a configurable fraction (default 10%) of capacity every minute.
4. Queue-estimate: When queueing a request, include X-Redwood-Queue-Estimate-ms in response headers with a 95th percentile estimate. If the estimate exceeds client max_latency_ms, evaluate fallback immediately.
5. Fallback policy selection: Respond with X-Redwood-Fallback-Policy when falling back (options: retry-with-backoff, accept-async-token, degrade-response, reject-with-retry-after).
6. Invariants: Priority may influence scheduling and batching, but not authorization or tenant-level billing semantics. Priority is advisory; servers must not change access control based on priority.

Client best practices

- Choose the least-permissive priority that meets user experience. Overusing realtime hurts overall system latency.
- Set max_latency_ms for interactive flows to provide a hard bound to the server.
- For multi-item batch requests set preserve_order only when required; otherwise allow server reordering to increase throughput.
- Respect server-provided fallback headers. If server suggests accept-async-token, use the provided async token to poll status rather than retrying immediately.

Operational metrics and dashboards

Essential metrics (per service & per priority class):
- requests_received_total{priority} (counter)
- requests_accepted_total{priority} (counter)
- requests_rejected_total{priority, reason} (counter) e.g., reason=overload, auth, malformed
- queue_estimate_ms_p95{priority} (gauge/histogram)
- average_processing_latency_ms{priority} (histogram)
- fallback_invocations_total{policy, priority} (counter)

Suggested SLOs (example)

- realtime: 99.9% of requests < 50ms server-side latency (excluding network).
- interactive: 99% < 150ms.
- standard: 95% < 500ms.
- bulk/background: No strict latency SLO; require throughput and completion-time monitoring.

Alerting thresholds (examples)

- queue_estimate_ms_p95{interactive} > 500ms for 5m -> page oncall and run overload playbook.
- fallback_invocations_total{reject-with-retry-after} increases > 5x baseline in 15m -> open incident.

Rollout and migration plan

1. Phase 0 — instrumentation only (2 weeks): Accept header, emit metrics but treat all requests as standard for scheduling.
2. Phase 1 — opt-in scheduling (4 weeks): Default behavior unchanged, opt into priority-aware scheduling for selected internal teams. Collect client-side adoption metrics.
3. Phase 2 — gradual enforcement (6 weeks): Honor priority hints for admission control with non-blocking fallbacks. Start returning X-Redwood-Queue-Estimate-ms to callers.
4. Phase 3 — production enforcement (8 weeks): Full scheduling enforcement, background/bulk reservation, and client guidance via SDK defaults.

Migration notes

- Backwards compatibility: Clients that do not send hints must continue to function.
- SDKs: Provide safe defaults in Redwood SDKs (JS, Python, Go). Default to setting X-Redwood-Priority based on callsite helpers (e.g., client.chat.sendInteractive()).
- Canary testing: Use 10% traffic window per region with canary metrics: p95 latency, fallback rate, and error budget burn.

Compatibility and security considerations

- Do not use priority headers for tenant isolation or billing. Treat as non-authoritative.
- Sanitize and rate-limit header size; accept only allowed tokens.
- Logging: redacted in logs; store only enum value. Avoid capturing client-provided free-form strings for privacy.

Ownership and governance

- Policy owner: Runtime Platform team (eng-platform) — responsible for enforcement, metrics, and SDK guidance.
- Specification owner: API Standards working group.
- Review cadence: Annual or when major service changes occur.

Examples and snippets

Example: interactive chat request (curl)

curl -X POST https://api.redwood.example/v1/chat 
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' 
  -H 'X-Redwood-Priority: interactive' 
  -d '{"messages": [{"role":"user","content":"Summarize the last policy meeting."}], "max_latency_ms": 200 }'

Server response headers (example)

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
X-Redwood-Accepted-Priority: interactive
X-Redwood-Queue-Estimate-ms: 18
X-Redwood-Fallback-Policy: none

Appendix: sample admission controller pseudocode

1. function admit(request):
2.   p = request.priority or 'standard'
3.   if load > high && p == 'background':
4.     return reject_with_policy('retry-with-backoff', 503)
5.   estimate = queue_estimator.predict(p)
6.   if request.max_latency_ms and estimate > request.max_latency_ms:
7.     return respond_with_policy('accept-async-token')
8.   enqueue(request, queue_for(p))
9.   return accepted
